E. Investment Implementation

11. Procurement (Strength—Medium; Effectiveness—Low, Reform priority—High)

62. Public procurement is essential to the efficient and effective delivery of modern infrastructure and public services with good governance and sustainable outcomes. Open competition and transparent procurement encourage all qualified providers to participate, increasing the likelihood of better value for money for public authorities. Well-functioning systems for monitoring procurement and independent procedures for dealing with procurement-related complaints can further support better outcomes and build trust in the government.

63. Open, competitive bidding is the default method of procurement in Namibia, there is a complaints review process, but no database to monitor the system. The legal framework requires that procurement opportunities are publicly advertised.^{^{33}} Although there are no barriers to participation in the public procurement market, the Public Procurement Act requires that for all procurement under international and national competitive bidding, prescribed incentives and conditions must be used to promote partnerships, joint venture arrangements and to require foreign entities to team up with Namibian bidders. These provisions are not sufficiently clear and undermine transparency in the procurement framework. There is a procurement portal for publishing annual procurement plans, procurement notices and contract award information. Bidders have the right to submit complaints during the procurement process and these must be reviewed within 14 days and the outcome published within seven days.

64. In practice, there is high usage of direct selection, no effective monitoring of the procurement system, and delays in publishing outcomes of the complaints review process. Conditions for use of less competitive/non-competitive methods are broadly drafted with significant levels of discretion, raising the possibility of inappropriate use or over-use.^{^{34}} For high-value contracts, which includes infrastructure, an average of 50 percent by contract value were open advertised bidding between 2018–2021 (Figure 24).^{^{35}} There is also a high rate of contract extension, further undermining competitive forces (Figure 25). The effectiveness of monitoring is undermined by weak contract management and the lack of a database with procurement information including contract completion times, final contract amounts and timelines of payments. While the procurement system generates a lot of information and data, there is no functioning database to systematically collect and monitor the procurement system. The Act requires public entities to submit procurement reports to the Procurement Policy Unit, but compliance is very low, with only 171 reports out of a possible 521 received from public entities during the financial year 2022/23.^{^{36}} Decisions by the Complaints Review Panel are not always published on the procurement portal within seven working days of the Review Panel’s decision, thus reducing transparency in the operation of the procurement system.
